Vignette: Harbhajan, Age 76

Harbhajan has spent the better part of fifty years working with his hands. Even now, well past the age when most men have put down their tools, he takes on small electrical jobs in his neighborhood - rewiring a kitchen outlet, replacing a breaker panel for a family he has known for decades. The work keeps him sharp, he says, and it gives him a reason to leave the house. That last part matters more than it used to.

Fourteen months ago, Harbhajan was walking back to his van after finishing a job in the early evening. It was still light out, barely. He had his toolbag over one shoulder and was thinking about dinner when two men came up behind him quickly. One grabbed his bag. The other shoved him hard into a parked car and held something against his back - he never saw what it was, but he believed it was a knife. They took his bag, his wallet, and his phone, and then they were gone. The whole thing lasted perhaps forty seconds. He stood alone on the pavement afterward, his heart hammering, his palms flat against the cold metal of the car door, unable to move for what felt like a very long time.

He did not tell his wife Parveen the full truth that night. He said he had been jostled, that someone had grabbed his bag. He did not describe the feeling of being held against the car, the breath of the man behind him, the absolute certainty in that moment that he was about to be seriously hurt or killed. He had lived through Partition as a small child, had carried fragments of that chaos quietly for decades, and he had always believed himself to be a man who did not make much of difficult things. This, he told himself, would pass.

It has not passed. He still goes to work, but he plans his jobs carefully now - nothing that runs past four in the afternoon, nothing in certain parts of the city. He parks as close as he can to wherever he is going and moves quickly between his van and the door. He finds himself scanning faces on the street in a way that exhausts him. When someone walks too close behind him, his body responds before his mind does - his shoulders lock, his breath shortens, and for a second or two he is back against that car. He does not always know what has triggered it until it is already happening.

Sleep has become unreliable. He wakes in the early hours, sometimes from dreams he cannot quite hold onto, sometimes from nothing at all, already alert and uneasy. Parveen has noticed. She reaches for his hand in the dark and he lets her take it, though he does not explain what woke him. He is not a man who has ever found it easy to speak about fear, and at seventy-six, with grandchildren who look up to him and a wife who has always depended on his steadiness, he is not sure how to begin.

What troubles him most, he says quietly, is not the fear itself but the way it has changed his sense of himself. He built a life in this country with those hands. He raised children, built a business, learned to navigate a world that was not always welcoming to him, and he did it without flinching. He had always felt capable - competent in a deep, physical way that his work made concrete every single day. Now he stands in a customer's kitchen and finds himself listening for footsteps in the hallway, checking the window, calculating how far he is from the door. The tools in his hands feel the same. He is the one who has changed, and he does not entirely recognize the man he has become.
